title: Nora's Splashy Map Adventure
markdown:
The sky above Sunny Meadow was a soft watery grey, like a blanket that had decided to be useful. Fat raindrops pattered on the windows of Nora the fox’s den. Inside: dried flowers, warm biscuits, a tail that twitched when she thought of puddles. Rain meant splashes, and splashes were delightful in theory. Wet paws were not. She hopped the biggest puddles with a stiff little shiver that made her whiskers argue. Sometimes a wide one was a bigger job than it looked, and she landed with a wobble she preferred not to discuss.

One afternoon, blackberry still on her tongue, she heard whispers from the village green. The yearly Puddle-Jumping Championship had changed its prize. Not highest jump, not furthest spray. This year: the best rainy-day map — driest routes, or the most honestly splashy ones, drawn so other paws could choose. Nora’s ears went up like flags. She loved maps: wiggly paths, friendly trees, the sort of drawing that made a place feel already visited. And perhaps, if she drew the safest least-wet ways, she could be useful without getting damp.

She hurried to Bram the badger, who was in his neat burrow cleaning his glasses with a scrap of fluff. “I’m entering the map competition.”

Bram blinked, kind and clever. “A good idea. Do you need help?”

“I can make the paths pretty. I am less good at knowing which puddle is a liar. You’re sensible.”

He adjusted the glasses until they gleamed. “Sensible is my middle name. Though it’s actually Bartholomew. You may keep calling me Bram.” He tapped a worn notebook. “We start by looking.”

They spent days over her drawings and his notes, walking the meadow in boots Bram insisted on and Nora tolerated. She put cheerful raindrops and smiling suns in the margins, and a tiny fox on a stepping stone who looked braver than she felt. Bram, calm as a still pond, would say, “This path goes through what the voles call the Great Soggy Swamp. Their tunnels vote wet. Another way?” He showed her the vole spoil-heaps, the darker grass, the place where a stick sank further than pride. She blushed a warm foxy red and redrew, a little sad, then a little interested. Pretty was not the same as true, and true, it turned out, had its own sort of prettiness if you let the lines wiggle where the water actually went.

They named the safe stones after biscuits so she would remember them: Digestive, Shortbread, the slightly crumbling one they called Maybe. Bram measured depths with a marked twig and wrote Grade One through Grade Four in a hand so neat the rain would have been ashamed to smudge it. Nora learned that a puddle with a willow reflection was often kinder than a puddle with no reflection at all, which meant mud pretending to be a mirror.

Nearby, Taliesin Buck — a squirrel who always thought he knew best — sketched with a pleased grin and almost no puddles at all. He used a ruler. He hummed as if humming were evidence.

“He pretends they aren’t there,” Nora whispered. A small envy squirmed. Taliesin always looked sure, even when the ground under him shone.

Championship day arrived grey and promising, the sort of grey that had already signed a contract with drizzle. Mrs. Vale stood in the square under a colourful umbrella, a clipboard that had seen other years, and a smile that made even Taliesin’s blank paper look like an entry. Rabbits compared bootlaces. A vole committee inspected the starting line and declared it adequately damp. Nora showed a delicate map of dry paths and clever stepping stones, each one looking very safe, the Maybe stone drawn a little smaller than the others because honesty had begun to leak into the ink. “Lovely detail,” Mrs. Vale said. “Thought, too. Thought is rarer than pretty.”

Then the downpour arrived as if it had been waiting for an audience. The square became a shimmering lake. Taliesin held up a sheet that was mostly blank paper. “My map says stay indoors! Ha!”

Nora’s heart sank. She had not tested a single route. What if her pretty lines led into the deepest wet? Her paws felt suddenly damp. Her tail reached the ground and stayed there.

Bram watched her with those steady eyes and pointed his pencil at a large inviting puddle by a willow. “Grade Four Splash-Maker. Notes say a decent Fun-to-Wetness Balance.”

Nora looked at the ripple, then at her map, then at her own paws as if they might vote. She would not only draw it. She ran, a smaller run first, a hop that became a decision. Splash. Water to the knees, a magnificent spray, and it was not a disaster. It was interesting. Cold, yes, and loud, and her whiskers wore jewels for a moment. She giggled, shyness loosening with each step. She tried the next puddle along the willow, a Grade Three according to the twig, and found Bram’s Fun-to-Wetness Balance was not a joke he had invented to be kind. She pencilled both onto the dripping paper while the rain still had opinions.

She returned dripping and added bold lines and a note: The Glorious Glee-Splash Zone — recommended if you mean the fun. She smeared one cheerful sun on purpose so the paper would remember the weather. “The old map was pretty. This one has been walked.”

Mrs. Vale looked at the wet fox and the new ink, then at Taliesin’s indoor sheet, which the rain had begun to argue with. “Not just a map. A record.” Bram, who did not make speeches, made a small tick in the notebook beside Grade Four, as if the willow had passed.

Nora, who had spent years hopping, had found that a tested splash beats an imagined dry path. She logged swamp veto / blank-paper boast / Grade Four willow in Bram’s notebook, left Taliesin’s indoor route where indoor routes belong, and let Mrs. Vale pin the true map to the board while it was still dotted with honest weather. A rabbit asked for a copy of the Glee-Splash line. Nora, still dripping, drew it again, larger. The prize, when it came, felt like permission to get her paws wet on purpose.
